        <h2 id="overview"><i class="fas fa-brain"></i> 1. What is Threat Intelligence?</h2>

        <h3>Understanding the Basics</h3>
        <p>Imagine you're a store detective trying to catch shoplifters. It would help to know what past shoplifters
            looked like, what tactics they used, and which stores they hit recently. That's essentially what
            <strong>threat intelligence</strong> is for cybersecurity.
        </p>

        <p>Threat intelligence feeds are like a constantly updated "watch list" that tells your security tools:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>These IP addresses are known to be malicious (blocklist them)</li>
            <li>These website domains are running phishing scams (block or alert)</li>
            <li>Files with these signatures are malware (stop them from running)</li>
            <li>This is how the latest attack campaigns are operating (watch for this behavior)</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Think of it like this:</strong> If your firewall and antivirus
            are your security guards, threat intelligence is like giving them a constantly updated "FBI Most Wanted"
            list. Instead of just reacting to bad behavior, they can proactively block known bad actors before they
            cause damage.
        </div>

        <h3>Why Threat Intelligence Matters</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Without Threat Intel</th>
                    <th>With Threat Intel</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td>Your firewall only blocks what it's explicitly configured to block</td>
                    <td>Firewall automatically blocks thousands of known malicious IPs</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Antivirus relies only on signatures from that vendor</td>
                    <td>New malware hashes pushed from multiple sources within hours</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>Phishing detection is limited to major campaigns</td>
                    <td>Real-time phishing URL feeds block new threats immediately</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td>You find out about attacks after you're hit</td>
                    <td>Proactive detection: "This IP attacked another company yesterday"</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>What is an IOC? (Indicator of Compromise)</h3>
        <p>IOCs are the "fingerprints" of malicious activity. When security researchers analyze attacks, they
            document observable patterns that can identify the same attack elsewhere:</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>IP Address:</strong> The attacker's server (e.g., <code>185.141.27.xxx</code>)</li>
            <li><strong>Domain:</strong> Malicious website (e.g., <code>fake-update.com</code>)</li>
            <li><strong>File Hash:</strong> Unique fingerprint of malware (SHA256)</li>
            <li><strong>URL:</strong> Specific malicious page (e.g., phishing login page)</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Common Misconception:</strong> Threat intelligence
            is NOT just about blocking. Good threat intel also enriches your investigations. When you see a
            suspicious IP in your logs, threat intel can tell you: "This IP is associated with APT28, a Russian
            state-sponsored group known for targeting government organizations."
        </div>

        <h3>The Technical Definition</h3>
        <p><strong>Threat Intelligence (TI)</strong> is evidence-based knowledge about existing or emerging threats
            that helps organizations prevent, detect, and respond to cyber attacks. It ranges from tactical IOCs to
            strategic threat assessments.</p>

        <h3>Intelligence Levels</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Level</th>
                    <th>Description</th>
                    <th>Audience</th>
                    <th>Example</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Strategic</strong></td>
                    <td>High-level trends, threat actors, motivations</td>
                    <td>Executives, CISO</td>
                    <td>"China-based attacks on semiconductor companies up 40%"</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Operational</strong></td>
                    <td>TTPs, campaigns, threat actor profiles</td>
                    <td>Security managers</td>
                    <td>"APT41 is targeting VPN vulnerabilities with this campaign"</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Tactical</strong></td>
                    <td>IOCs: IPs, domains, hashes, URLs</td>
                    <td>SOC analysts, SIEM</td>
                    <td>"Block these 500 C2 domains immediately"</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Technical</strong></td>
                    <td>Malware analysis, exploit details</td>
                    <td>Malware analysts, IR</td>
                    <td>"This malware uses DLL sideloading via this technique"</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Where to Start:</strong> If you're new to threat
            intelligence, start with 3-5 free feeds (abuse.ch, AlienVault OTX, OpenPhish). Import them as lookup
            tables in your SIEM and create alerts when your logs match known-bad indicators. You'll be amazed what
            you find.
        </div>

        <h2 id="ioc-types"><i class="fas fa-fingerprint"></i> 2. IOC Types & Categories</h2>

        <h3>Common Indicator Types</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Type</th>
                    <th>Description</th>
                    <th>Example</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>IP Address</strong></td>
                    <td>Malicious C2, scanning, attacking IPs</td>
                    <td><code>185.141.27.xxx</code></td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Domain</strong></td>
                    <td>Malware C2, phishing domains</td>
                    <td><code>malicious-update.com</code></td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>URL</strong></td>
                    <td>Specific malicious URLs</td>
                    <td><code>hxxps://evil[.]com/payload[.]exe</code></td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>File Hash (MD5/SHA1/SHA256)</strong></td>
                    <td>Malware file signatures</td>
                    <td><code>44d88612fea8a...</code></td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Email Address</strong></td>
                    <td>Phishing sender addresses</td>
                    <td><code>ceo@fake-company.com</code></td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>CVE</strong></td>
                    <td>Exploited vulnerabilities</td>
                    <td><code>CVE-2024-21887</code></td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>YARA Rule</strong></td>
                    <td>Pattern-based malware detection</td>
                    <td>Rule definitions</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>JA3/JA3S</strong></td>
                    <td>TLS fingerprints</td>
                    <td>Client/server TLS signatures</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2 id="feeds"><i class="fas fa-database"></i> 3. Free & Commercial Feed Sources</h2>

        <h3>Free/Open Source Feeds</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Feed</th>
                    <th>Type</th>
                    <th>Format</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>abuse.ch (URLhaus, Feodo, MalwareBazaar)</strong></td>
                    <td>Malware, Botnets</td>
                    <td>CSV, JSON, API</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>AlienVault OTX</strong></td>
                    <td>Community IOCs</td>
                    <td>STIX, CSV, API</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>OpenPhish</strong></td>
                    <td>Phishing URLs</td>
                    <td>Text, JSON</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>PhishTank</strong></td>
                    <td>Phishing URLs</td>
                    <td>CSV, XML, JSON</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Emerging Threats</strong></td>
                    <td>IDS rules, IPs</td>
                    <td>Suricata/Snort rules</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>SANS ISC</strong></td>
                    <td>Suspicious IPs</td>
                    <td>Text</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>CISA KEV</strong></td>
                    <td>Exploited CVEs</td>
                    <td>JSON, CSV</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>Commercial Feeds</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Recorded Future, Mandiant, CrowdStrike (Premium TI)</li>
            <li>VirusTotal (File/URL analysis)</li>
            <li>DomainTools, RiskIQ (Domain/infrastructure intel)</li>
            <li>Palo Alto Unit 42, Cisco Talos (Vendor TI)</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="stix-taxii"><i class="fas fa-exchange-alt"></i> 4. STIX/TAXII Standards</h2>
        <p>STIX and TAXII are OASIS standards for sharing threat intelligence:</p>

        <h3>STIX (Structured Threat Information eXpression)</h3>
        <p>A language and serialization format for threat intelligence objects:</p>
        <pre><code>{

“type”: “indicator”, “id”: “indicator–a932fcc6-e032-176c-126f-cb970a5a1fff”, “pattern”: “[domain-name:value = ‘malicious.com’]”, “pattern_type”: “stix”, “valid_from”: “2025-01-01T00:00:00Z”, “labels”: [“malicious-activity”] }

        <h3>TAXII (Trusted Automated eXchange of Intelligence Information)</h3>
        <p>A protocol for exchanging STIX data. TAXII 2.1 uses REST APIs.</p>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>Collections:</strong> Groups of intelligence objects</li>
            <li><strong>Channels:</strong> Push-based intelligence sharing</li>
            <li><strong>Discovery:</strong> Find available TAXII services</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="integration"><i class="fas fa-plug"></i> 5. SIEM & Security Tool Integration</h2>

        <h3>Integration Methods</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Method</th>
                    <th>Best For</th>
                    <th>Complexity</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Lookup Tables</strong></td>
                    <td>Simple IOC matching</td>
                    <td>Low</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>API Integration</strong></td>
                    <td>Real-time enrichment</td>
                    <td>Medium</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>TAXII Client</strong></td>
                    <td>Standardized feed ingestion</td>
                    <td>Medium</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>TIP Integration</strong></td>
                    <td>Aggregating multiple feeds</td>
                    <td>High</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>Splunk Integration Example</h3>
        <pre><code># Create lookup table from threat feed

| inputlookup threat_ips.csv | eval threat_type=“malicious_ip”

Correlate with logs

index=firewall | lookup threat_ips.csv ip as dest_ip OUTPUT threat_type | where isnotnull(threat_type)

        <h3>Firewall/Proxy Integration</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Import IP/domain blocklists automatically</li>
            <li>Create EDL (External Dynamic Lists) for Palo Alto</li>
            <li>Feed proxy URL categories with threat data</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="tip"><i class="fas fa-server"></i> 6. Threat Intelligence Platforms (TIPs)</h2>
        <p>A TIP aggregates, normalizes, and operationalizes threat intelligence from multiple sources.</p>

        <h3>Popular TIP Solutions</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Platform</th>
                    <th>Type</th>
                    <th>Key Features</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>MISP</strong></td>
                    <td>Open Source</td>
                    <td>Sharing, correlation, STIX/TAXII</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>OpenCTI</strong></td>
                    <td>Open Source</td>
                    <td>Knowledge management, STIX native</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>TheHive/Cortex</strong></td>
                    <td>Open Source</td>
                    <td>Case management + enrichment</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Anomali ThreatStream</strong></td>
                    <td>Commercial</td>
                    <td>Enterprise TIP</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>ThreatConnect</strong></td>
                    <td>Commercial</td>
                    <td>TIP + orchestration</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2 id="workflow"><i class="fas fa-project-diagram"></i> 7. Operational Workflow</h2>

        <h3>Threat Intel Operational Cycle</h3>
        <ol>
            <li><strong>Collect:</strong> Ingest feeds from multiple sources</li>
            <li><strong>Normalize:</strong> Convert to common format (STIX)</li>
            <li><strong>Enrich:</strong> Add context (WHOIS, geolocation, related IOCs)</li>
            <li><strong>Analyze:</strong> Correlate and prioritize</li>
            <li><strong>Disseminate:</strong> Push to detection tools (SIEM, FW, EDR)</li>
            <li><strong>Act:</strong> Alert, block, or investigate matches</li>
            <li><strong>Feedback:</strong> Improve based on false positive rates</li>
        </ol>

        <h2 id="quality"><i class="fas fa-check-double"></i> 8. Feed Quality & Confidence</h2>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Quality Matters:</strong> Not all threat feeds are
            equal. Poor quality feeds lead to alert fatigue and false positives. Always assign confidence levels and
            track feed performance.
        </div>

        <h3>Confidence Scoring</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>High (80-100%):</strong> Verified by multiple sources, recent, active</li>
            <li><strong>Medium (40-79%):</strong> Single source, reasonable age, some validation</li>
            <li><strong>Low (0-39%):</strong> Old data, unverified, high false positive rate</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Feed Hygiene</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Set expiration dates on IOCs (30-90 days typical)</li>
            <li>Track false positive rates per feed</li>
            <li>Deduplicate across feeds</li>
            <li>Retire underperforming feeds</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="automation"><i class="fas fa-robot"></i> 9. Automation & Enrichment</h2>

        <h3>Automated Enrichment</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>VirusTotal:</strong> File/URL reputation</li>
            <li><strong>Shodan:</strong> IP service discovery</li>
            <li><strong>WHOIS:</strong> Domain registration</li>
            <li><strong>GeoIP:</strong> Location data</li>
            <li><strong>PassiveDNS:</strong> Historical domain resolution</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>SOAR Integration</h3>
        <p>Use SOAR platforms to automate threat intel workflows:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>Auto-enrich IOCs on detection</li>
            <li>Auto-block confirmed malicious indicators</li>
            <li>Auto-create tickets for investigation</li>
            <li>Auto-update feeds and blocklists</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Quick Start Checklist:</strong>
            <ol style="margin-top: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 0;">
                <li>Start with 3-5 high-quality free feeds</li>
                <li>Create lookup tables in your SIEM</li>
                <li>Build correlation rules for IOC matches</li>
                <li>Track false positive rates</li>
                <li>Consider MISP or OpenCTI if scaling</li>
            </ol>
        </div>
